objective: Elevating organizational project management (OPM): assessing current competencies, building a tailored competency framework, and pairing mentoring with performance management
secondaryObjectives: Cultivating OPM capabilities: identifying and prioritizing the capabilities the organization actually needs, then closing people/process/technology gaps

sources.cite: PMI, PMI PMO Certified Professional (PMI-PMOCP) Examination Content Outline and Specifications, January 2025 (v2): Organizational Development and Alignment 16%, PMO Strategic Elements 18%, PMO Design and Structuring 18%, PMO Operation and Performance 15%, PMO Enhancement and Effectiveness 18%, People 15%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a study page (masteryexamprep, dated 2025-12-20) that cites PMI's outline of January 2025 (v2) for these weights. The page lists no task statements; it says questions reward 'governance realism: decision rights, thresholds, escalation paths, and reporting that drives decisions'. PMI's PDF (the course seed cites it) was not opened; the task wording is the course seed's, to verify. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's water-utility-rebalance-pmipmocp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You lead the PMO at Calder Engineering, a fictional engineering consultancy. Projects overrun often; the CEO wants 'better project managers'.
handover: Sixty project managers, from new graduates to 20-year veterans.
No competency framework; training is a generic course.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: after the course, overruns from unpriced changes continue unchanged.
Week 3: the new tool goes live; changes are still accepted without orders.
Week 4: two strong project managers resign after being ranked low on commercial skills.

framePrompt.title: Generic or tailored?
framePrompt.context: A generic framework is available off the shelf.

choices.label: Tailor a framework to the consultancy: technical, commercial and leadership competencies by level, weighted to the gaps found
choices.feedback: A tailored competency framework targets what the organization actually needs.

choices.label: Adopt the generic framework
choices.feedback: It doesn't emphasize the commercial gap.

choices.label: Skip the framework and send everyone on the course
Prioritize change control: train commercial skills, add a change-order process, and a change log in the project tool

effects.log: Change control is the priority across people, process and tools.

choices.feedback: Capabilities are prioritized by need and gaps closed across people, process and technology.

choices.label: Train commercial skills only
choices.feedback: Without a process and a tool, skills don't change outcomes.

choices.label: Buy a new project tool
choices.feedback: A tool doesn't fix unpriced changes.

mentorPrompt.title: Mentoring and reviews
mentorPrompt.context: Veterans could mentor; reviews don't mention competencies.

choices.label: Pair each project manager with a mentor, set development goals from the framework, and include them in performance reviews

effects.log: Mentoring and reviews use the framework.

choices.feedback: Mentoring paired with performance management turns a framework into growth.

choices.label: Rank project managers by the framework and publish the list
choices.feedback: Public ranking breeds fear and gaming, not growth.

reflection.question: Write the OPM capability plan summary for the CEO.

parts.label: Assessment and framework
parts.criteria: Commercial gap; 70% of overruns from unpriced changes; tailored framework.
parts.modelAnswer: Our managers plan well but price changes poorly; 70% of overruns trace to unpriced changes. The framework is weighted to that gap.

parts.label: Closing the gap
parts.criteria: Change control across people, process and tools; mentoring tied to reviews.
parts.modelAnswer: Change control is the priority: training, a change-order process and a change log; mentors and reviews follow the framework.

expertPath.text: Assess competencies and overrun causes first.
Tailor the framework to the assessed gaps.
Prioritize change control across people, process and tools.
Pair mentoring with framework-based development goals in reviews.

scoring.modelReasoning: Organizational project management grows from an assessment of current competencies, a framework tailored to the organization's needs, capabilities prioritized by what drives results and closed across people, process and technology, and mentoring paired with performance management rather than rankings.
